modules.name: Access
modules.header:
Alignment, unaligned access, byte swapping, and clearing a secret so that it stays cleared.
Three of these exist because a pointer is not always where a type wants it. A value read from a file, a packet or
a mapped structure sits wherever the format put it, and on some machines a load that crosses an alignment boundary
faults rather than being slow. The load and store helpers below go through bytes, so they are correct at any
address and cost the same everywhere.
`ZeroizeBlock` exists because clearing a secret is a write nothing reads back, which is exactly the write a
compiler is entitled to delete. It is the one operation here that rests on a compiler guarantee rather than a
library one.

modules.name: Alloc
modules.header:
Taking storage from the operating system, at whatever granularity it hands it out in.
The one allocation primitive under `Rux/Allocator`, and deliberately the smallest possible: it takes bytes
and gives back an address, with no size class, no free list and no header of its own beyond what the
platform needs to release the block again. Everything shaped like an allocator is built on this rather
than inside it.
A zero size returns null rather than an address, which is the one place this differs from the page layer
above it: `Rux/Allocator` gives a zero-sized request a shared non-null address so that no caller has to
branch, and does that itself.

modules.name: Block
modules.header:
Raw block operations: copying, moving, filling, comparing and searching a run of bytes.
Nothing here knows what the bytes mean. A block is an address and a length, and every operation touches exactly
the length it is given and nothing beyond it.
**Zero length is always legal, and null is legal with it.** A length of zero does nothing at all, and the pointers
are not examined, so `Copy(null, null, 0)` is defined and does nothing. That is deliberately not C's rule, where
passing null to `memcpy` is undefined even for a zero length — a rule that turns an ordinary empty case into a
trap and forces every caller to guard. A non-zero length requires real, usable storage.
Overlap is where `Copy` and `Move` part company. `Copy` may be read as copying byte zero first and byte `length -
1` last, so a destination that overlaps the source ahead of it reads bytes the copy has already overwritten.
`Move` is defined for every overlap, at the cost of choosing a direction first.
The comparisons treat a byte as unsigned, so ordering does not depend on whether the platform's plain `char` is
signed. None of them is constant-time: each stops at the first difference, so nothing here may compare a secret.

modules.name: Free
modules.header:
Giving storage back to the operating system.
A null pointer is accepted and does nothing, so a cleanup path need not test for one. Everything else must
be an address this module's `Alloc` or `Realloc` returned; there is no way to check that here and no
attempt to.

modules.name: Pages
modules.header:
Address space at the granularity the operating system hands it out in: whole pages, with a protection.
This is the layer under an allocator rather than an allocator itself. Nothing here tracks what it gave out, keeps
a free list, or remembers a length — a caller releases exactly what it took, and passing a different length is
its own mistake to make.
The four systems disagree about almost everything here, so the surface is one this package defines rather than any
one platform's. Protection is a flag set, failure is a `PageError` rather than an errno or a `GetLastError` code,
and a length is rounded up to whole pages by the system whether or not the caller does it first.
Windows is the one that differs in kind. It separates reserving address space from committing storage to it, and
these calls always do both — which is the behaviour every other system has and the one an allocator expects. A
caller wanting a large reservation cheaply has to reach for `Rux/Windows` directly.

modules.name: Realloc
modules.header:
Resizing an allocation, preserving the bytes that still fit.
Three degenerate cases, each answered rather than refused: a null pointer allocates, a zero size releases
and returns null, and a failure returns null while leaving the original allocation valid and still the
caller's. That last one is the one callers get wrong — assigning the result over the original pointer
loses the allocation on every failure — and is why the failure is documented on every path here.

items.name: IsAligned
items.signature: pub func IsAligned(address: uint, alignment: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `address` is a multiple of `alignment`.
doc.markdown:
Whether `address` is a multiple of `alignment`.
`address` and `alignment` are read by value. An `alignment` of zero reports false rather than dividing by it, and
an alignment that is not a power of two gives an answer that is arithmetically true but rarely meaningful, since
hardware alignment is always a power of two.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: address
params.markdown: the address or offset to test

params.name: alignment
params.markdown: the boundary to test against; zero reports false

items.name: IsPointerAligned
items.signature: pub func IsPointerAligned(pointer: *opaque, alignment: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `pointer` is aligned for `alignment`.
doc.markdown:
Whether `pointer` is aligned for `alignment`.
`pointer` is read by value and never dereferenced. A null pointer reports true for every alignment, since zero is
a multiple of everything; a caller that means "usable" has to ask that separately.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: pointer
params.markdown: the address to test, never dereferenced

items.name: AlignUp
items.signature: pub func AlignUp(value: uint, alignment: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: The next multiple of `alignment` at or above `value`.
doc.markdown:
The next multiple of `alignment` at or above `value`.
`value` and `alignment` are read by value. An `alignment` of zero or one returns `value` unchanged, since every
value is already a multiple of both.
Returns `value` itself when it is already aligned, so this is idempotent.
A `value` within `alignment - 1` of the maximum has no next multiple, and this wraps to a small number rather
than reporting it. A caller sizing an allocation must check for that before trusting the result; `AlignUpChecked`
does the checking.

params.name: alignment
params.markdown: the boundary to round to; zero or one changes nothing

doc.returns: the next multiple of `alignment` at or above `value`

items.name: AlignUpChecked
items.signature: pub func AlignUpChecked(value: uint, alignment: uint, result: *var uint) -> bool

doc.summary: The next multiple of `alignment` at or above `value`, reporting whether it was representable.
doc.markdown:
The next multiple of `alignment` at or above `value`, reporting whether it was representable.
`value` and `alignment` are read by value; `result` receives the aligned value when this returns `false`, and is
left unwritten when it returns `true`. `result` must not be null.
Returns `true` when rounding up would pass the maximum, which is the case an allocation size has to notice: a
wrapped size is an allocation far smaller than the caller asked for.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: alignment
params.markdown: the boundary to round to; zero or one changes nothing

params.name: result
params.markdown: receives the aligned value when this returns false

doc.returns: true when rounding up would pass the maximum

items.name: AlignDown
items.signature: pub func AlignDown(value: uint, alignment: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: The previous multiple of `alignment` at or below `value`.
doc.markdown:
The previous multiple of `alignment` at or below `value`.
`value` and `alignment` are read by value. An `alignment` of zero or one returns `value` unchanged.
Cannot fail: rounding down never leaves the range.

params.name: alignment
params.markdown: the boundary to round to; zero or one changes nothing

doc.returns: the previous multiple of `alignment` at or below `value`

items.name: LoadUnaligned
items.signature: pub func LoadUnaligned<T>(source: *opaque, destination: *var T)

doc.summary: Reads a value of `T` from `source`, whatever `source` is aligned to.
doc.markdown:
Reads a value of `T` from `source`, whatever `source` is aligned to.
`source` is borrowed and `sizeof(T)` bytes are read from it; `destination` receives the value. Both must be
non-null.
The bytes are taken one at a time, so this is correct at any address on any machine — including the ones where a
misaligned load faults rather than merely costing more.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `sizeof(T)` and allocates nothing.
`source` must be readable for `sizeof(T)` bytes. The bytes are taken as they are, so a value that is not a valid
`T` stays invalid; this reinterprets rather than validating.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: the type whose bytes are read

params.name: source
params.markdown: the address to read `sizeof(T)` bytes from, at any alignment

items.name: StoreUnaligned
items.signature: pub func StoreUnaligned<T>(destination: *var opaque, value: *T)

doc.summary: Writes a value of `T` to `destination`, whatever `destination` is aligned to.
doc.markdown:
Writes a value of `T` to `destination`, whatever `destination` is aligned to.
`value` is borrowed and read; `destination` is borrowed and receives `sizeof(T)` bytes. Both must be non-null.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `sizeof(T)` and allocates nothing.
`destination` must be writable for `sizeof(T)` bytes.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: the type whose bytes are written

params.name: destination
params.markdown: the address to write `sizeof(T)` bytes to, at any alignment

items.name: ReverseBlock
items.signature: pub func ReverseBlock(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint)

doc.summary: Reverses the order of `length` bytes at `buffer`, in place.
doc.markdown:
Reverses the order of `length` bytes at `buffer`, in place.
`buffer` is borrowed and rewritten. A `length` of zero or one changes nothing and accepts a null pointer at zero.
This is the byte-order conversion for a run of bytes rather than for one value; `Core::ReverseBytes` is the one
that takes an integer.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be readable and writable for `length` bytes.

params.name: buffer
params.markdown: the bytes to reverse in place

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes; zero or one changes nothing

items.name: LoadLittleEndian
items.signature: pub func LoadLittleEndian<T>(source: *opaque, destination: *var T)

doc.summary: Reads a `T` from `source`, taking the bytes as little-endian.
doc.markdown:
Reads a `T` from `source`, taking the bytes as little-endian.
`source` is borrowed and `sizeof(T)` bytes are read; `destination` receives the value in the target's own order.
Both must be non-null. Needs no alignment.
This is the pair of calls a file or wire format actually needs: the bytes are wherever the format put them, and
their order is the format's rather than the machine's.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `sizeof(T)` and allocates nothing.
`source` must be readable for `sizeof(T)` bytes.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: the type whose bytes are read

params.name: source
params.markdown: the address to read `sizeof(T)` little-endian bytes from

params.name: destination
params.markdown: receives the value in the target's own order

items.name: LoadBigEndian
items.signature: pub func LoadBigEndian<T>(source: *opaque, destination: *var T)

doc.summary: Reads a `T` from `source`, taking the bytes as big-endian.
doc.markdown:
Reads a `T` from `source`, taking the bytes as big-endian.
`source` is borrowed and `sizeof(T)` bytes are read; `destination` receives the value in the target's own order.
Both must be non-null. Needs no alignment. This is network byte order.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `sizeof(T)` and allocates nothing.
`source` must be readable for `sizeof(T)` bytes.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: the type whose bytes are read

params.name: source
params.markdown: the address to read `sizeof(T)` big-endian bytes from

params.name: destination
params.markdown: receives the value in the target's own order

items.name: StoreLittleEndian
items.signature: pub func StoreLittleEndian<T>(destination: *var opaque, value: *T)

doc.summary: Writes a `T` to `destination` as little-endian bytes.
doc.markdown:
Writes a `T` to `destination` as little-endian bytes.
`value` is borrowed and read; `destination` receives `sizeof(T)` bytes. Both must be non-null. Needs no
alignment.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `sizeof(T)` and allocates nothing.
`destination` must be writable for `sizeof(T)` bytes.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: the type whose bytes are written

items.name: StoreBigEndian
items.signature: pub func StoreBigEndian<T>(destination: *var opaque, value: *T)

doc.summary: Writes a `T` to `destination` as big-endian bytes.
doc.markdown:
Writes a `T` to `destination` as big-endian bytes.
`value` is borrowed and read; `destination` receives `sizeof(T)` bytes. Both must be non-null. Needs no
alignment.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `sizeof(T)` and allocates nothing.
`destination` must be writable for `sizeof(T)` bytes.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: the type whose bytes are written

items.name: ZeroizeBlock
items.signature: pub func ZeroizeBlock(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint)

doc.summary: Clears `length` bytes at `buffer`, and is not removed however unread those bytes are afterwards.
doc.markdown:
Clears `length` bytes at `buffer`, and is not removed however unread those bytes are afterwards.
`buffer` is borrowed and written. A `length` of zero writes nothing and accepts a null pointer.
This is what `Zero` is not. Clearing a secret is a write nothing reads back, which dead-store elimination is
entitled to delete, and ordinary source cannot say "and mean it" — so this is a compiler guarantee rather than a
library one.
The guarantee is `Core::Zeroize`'s; this adds the empty-case contract the rest of this module has and takes the
`*var opaque` and `uint` every other block operation here takes.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes.
It clears the storage it is given and nothing else. A copy the caller made beforehand, a value the compiler
spilled to the stack, or bytes a reallocation left behind are all still there — so a secret has to be kept in
one place from the start for this to be the whole of its erasure.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes; zero writes nothing and accepts a null pointer

items.name: Alloc
items.signature: pub func Alloc(size: uint) -> *var opaque

doc.summary: Allocates `size` uninitialized bytes.
doc.markdown:
Allocates `size` uninitialized bytes.
Returns the base address, or null when the size overflows the platform bookkeeping or the system cannot satisfy
the request. A zero size is permitted, but the returned address is platform-dependent and must not be touched.
The allocation is owned by the caller until `Free` releases it or `Realloc` replaces it. The address is aligned
to at least 16 bytes on every supported target.
The bytes are uninitialized. Reading any byte before writing it, accessing beyond `size`, or using the address
after it is released is invalid.

params.name: size
params.markdown: how many bytes to take; zero returns null

doc.returns: the address of the allocation, or null when the system refused

items.name: Copy
items.signature: pub func Copy(destination: *var opaque, source: *opaque, length: uint)

doc.summary: Copies `length` bytes from `source` to `destination`, which must not overlap.
doc.markdown:
Copies `length` bytes from `source` to `destination`, which must not overlap.
`source` is borrowed and read; `destination` is borrowed and written. Nothing is returned and nothing takes
ownership. A `length` of zero copies nothing and accepts null for either pointer.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`destination` must be writable for `length` bytes and `source` readable for `length`, and the two ranges must not
overlap. Use `Move` when they might: this one is free to copy in whichever order suits the machine.

params.name: destination
params.markdown: where the bytes go; must not overlap `source`

items.name: Move
items.signature: pub func Move(destination: *var opaque, source: *opaque, length: uint)

doc.summary: Copies `length` bytes from `source` to `destination`, correctly even when the two overlap.
doc.markdown:
Copies `length` bytes from `source` to `destination`, correctly even when the two overlap.
`source` is borrowed and read; `destination` is borrowed and written. A `length` of zero moves nothing and
accepts null for either pointer.
The result is what copying through a temporary would give: every source byte reaches its destination as it was
before the move began. Sliding a run forward within one buffer therefore works, which is what an insertion into
the middle of an array needs.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing — the temporary is notional, and the
direction of the copy is what actually makes it right.
`destination` must be writable for `length` bytes and `source` readable for `length`. They may overlap in any
way, including exactly.

params.name: destination
params.markdown: where the bytes go; may overlap `source`

items.name: Set
items.signature: pub func Set(destination: *var opaque, value: byte, length: uint)

doc.summary: Writes `value` to each of `length` bytes at `destination`.
doc.markdown:
Writes `value` to each of `length` bytes at `destination`.
`destination` is borrowed and written. A `length` of zero writes nothing and accepts a null pointer.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`destination` must be writable for `length` bytes. This is not the call for clearing a secret: a write nothing
reads back may be deleted, and `Core::Zeroize` is the one that may not be.

params.name: value
params.markdown: the byte to write to each

items.name: Zero
items.signature: pub func Zero(destination: *var opaque, length: uint)

doc.summary: Writes zero to each of `length` bytes at `destination`.
doc.markdown:
Writes zero to each of `length` bytes at `destination`.
`destination` is borrowed and written. A `length` of zero writes nothing and accepts a null pointer.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`destination` must be writable for `length` bytes. For a secret, use `Core::Zeroize`, which the compiler may not
delete however unread the bytes are afterwards.

items.name: MismatchOffset
items.signature: pub func MismatchOffset(left: *opaque, right: *opaque, length: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: The offset at which two blocks first differ, or `length` when they do not.
doc.markdown:
The offset at which two blocks first differ, or `length` when they do not.
Both pointers are borrowed and read. A `length` of zero reports zero and accepts null for either pointer, which
is the same answer two equal empty blocks give.
The answer is a position rather than an ordering, so it says where the blocks diverge and not which one sorts
first. `Compare` answers that.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the shared prefix and allocates nothing.
Both pointers must be readable for `length` bytes. Not constant-time: it stops at the first difference, so it
must not be used on a secret.
doc.returns: the offset of the first differing byte, or `length` when none differs

items.name: Compare
items.signature: pub func Compare(left: *opaque, right: *opaque, length: uint) -> Ordering

doc.summary: Orders two blocks lexicographically, byte by byte.
doc.markdown:
Orders two blocks lexicographically, byte by byte.
Both pointers are borrowed and read. Returns `Less` when `left` sorts first, `Greater` when `right` does, and
`Equal` when the two ranges hold the same bytes. A `length` of zero reports `Equal` and accepts null for either
pointer.
Bytes are compared as unsigned, so the answer does not depend on whether the platform's plain `char` is signed,
and it matches the order the bytes would sort in as a string.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the shared prefix and allocates nothing.
Both pointers must be readable for `length` bytes. Not constant-time: it stops at the first difference, so a
secret compared this way leaks where it differs. `Rux/Crypto` is where a constant-time comparison belongs.

items.name: Equal
items.signature: pub func Equal(left: *opaque, right: *opaque, length: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether two blocks hold the same bytes.
doc.markdown:
Whether two blocks hold the same bytes.
Both pointers are borrowed and read. A `length` of zero reports true and accepts null for either pointer: two
empty blocks are equal.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the shared prefix and allocates nothing.
Both pointers must be readable for `length` bytes. Not constant-time.

items.name: Find
items.signature: pub func Find(haystack: *opaque, length: uint, value: byte) -> uint

doc.summary: The offset of the first byte equal to `value`, or `length` when there is none.
doc.markdown:
The offset of the first byte equal to `value`, or `length` when there is none.
`haystack` is borrowed and read. A `length` of zero reports zero and accepts a null pointer, which is also what a
search that found nothing reports — an empty block contains nothing to find either way.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the offset returned and allocates nothing.
`haystack` must be readable for `length` bytes.
doc.returns: the offset of the first occurrence, or `length` when there is none

items.name: Free
items.signature: pub func Free(ptr: *opaque)

doc.summary: Releases an allocation.
doc.markdown:
Releases an allocation. A null pointer is accepted and does nothing.
A non-null `ptr` must be the live base address returned by `Alloc` or `Realloc`. Every pointer into the block
becomes invalid immediately; releasing an interior, foreign, or already released address is invalid.

params.name: ptr
params.markdown: an address `Alloc` or `Realloc` returned, or null

items.name: PageNone
items.signature: pub const PageNone: uint32

doc.summary: What may be done with a page, as a set of flags to combine with `|`.
doc.markdown:
What may be done with a page, as a set of flags to combine with `|`.
A protection of `PageNone` reserves the address space and refuses every access to it, which is how a guard page
is made. Combining write and execute is refused outright by some systems and by policy on others, so a caller
that needs both should write through one protection and execute through another.

items.name: PageRead
items.signature: pub const PageRead: uint32

doc.summary: The page may be read.
doc.markdown: The page may be read.

items.name: PageWrite
items.signature: pub const PageWrite: uint32

doc.summary: The page may be written.
doc.markdown:
The page may be written.
Implies readability on every supported system: none of them can make a page write-only, whatever their flags
suggest.

items.name: PageExecute
items.signature: pub const PageExecute: uint32

doc.summary: The page may be executed.
doc.markdown: The page may be executed.

items.name: PageError
items.signature: pub enum PageError

doc.summary: Why a page operation did not do what was asked.
doc.markdown:
Why a page operation did not do what was asked. `Copy`.
One set of reasons across four systems that report failure three different ways: an errno, a `GetLastError` code,
and a sentinel address. A reason the mapping does not cover arrives as `Failed`, which is not a promise that
nothing went wrong — only that this module could not name it. Every case is a failure: a call that succeeds
reports its success channel instead.

cases.name: InvalidLength
cases.doc: The length was zero, or too large for the address space to hold.

cases.name: InvalidAddress
cases.doc: The address was not page-aligned, or names nothing this process may operate on.

cases.name: OutOfMemory
cases.doc: The system has no storage to back the request.

cases.name: PermissionDenied
cases.doc: The system refused the protection asked for, which is usually write and execute together.

cases.name: Unsupported
cases.doc: The combination is not supported on this system.

cases.name: Failed
cases.doc: The system reported a failure this module has no name for.

items.name: MinimumPageSize
items.signature: pub const MinimumPageSize: uint

doc.summary: The smallest page any supported system uses, in bytes.
doc.markdown:
The smallest page any supported system uses, in bytes.
Four kibibytes, which is the page size on seven of the eight supported target cells and the floor on the eighth:
Apple Silicon uses sixteen, and a Linux kernel may be configured for sixteen or sixty-four, but none of them
goes below this.
It is a bound, not an answer. `PageAlign` rounds to it because rounding to a divisor of the real page size is
always safe — the system rounds again, up to whatever its pages actually are — and because asking the system on
every call would put a file read or a system call inside an allocator's inner loop. A caller that needs the real
granularity asks `PageSize` once and keeps the answer.

items.name: PageSize
items.signature: pub func PageSize() -> uint ! PageError

doc.summary: Asks the system how large a page actually is, in bytes.
doc.markdown:
Asks the system how large a page actually is, in bytes.
The answer is always a power of two, and is the granularity every call in this module rounds a length up to. It
varies by machine and not only by system: Apple Silicon uses sixteen kibibytes where Apple's x86-64 uses four,
and a Linux kernel may be configured for either or for sixty-four.
Each system is asked the way it wants to be asked, by the package that owns it — `GetSystemInfo` on Windows,
`getpagesize` on Darwin, the `hw.pagesize` sysctl on FreeBSD, and `/proc/self/auxv` on Linux, whose kernel
publishes the value in the auxiliary vector rather than behind a system call. Nothing is captured at process
start and no libc is called.
Reports `Unsupported` when the system would not answer — on Linux, a container built without `/proc` is the
ordinary way that happens. A failure is reported rather than a guess substituted, because a caller that is
asking this instead of using `MinimumPageSize` is asking for the real number, and a wrong real number is worse
than a refusal it can handle.
Allocates nothing. Runs in constant time on three systems and performs one open, read and close on Linux, so a
caller that needs the size more than once should keep it.
doc.returns: the page size in bytes, or the reason the system would not answer

items.name: PageAllocate
items.signature: pub func PageAllocate(length: uint, protection: uint32) -> (*var opaque) ! PageError

doc.summary: Takes `length` bytes of address space with the given protection, and reports where it landed.
doc.markdown:
Takes `length` bytes of address space with the given protection, and reports where it landed.
`length` is rounded up to whole pages by the system. `protection` is a combination of the `Page*` flags, and
`PageNone` is legal — it takes the space and refuses every access to it.
The pages are zero-filled on every supported system. Nothing else about their contents is promised.
A `length` of zero is refused with `InvalidLength` rather than succeeding with nothing, because a zero-length
mapping is a caller's arithmetic error far more often than an intention.
Runs in constant time as far as this module is concerned; the system may take longer. Allocates nothing beyond
what it is asked for.
The pages are the caller's until `PageRelease` takes exactly this length back. Releasing a different length, or
an address this did not return, is undefined on Windows and silently partial elsewhere.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes of address space to take, rounded up to whole pages by the system

params.name: protection
params.markdown: what may be done with the pages, as `Page*` flags

doc.returns: the base address of the pages, or the reason the address space was not taken

items.name: PageRelease
items.signature: pub func PageRelease(address: *var opaque, length: uint) -> ! PageError

doc.summary: Gives back `length` bytes of address space at `address`.
doc.markdown:
Gives back `length` bytes of address space at `address`.
`address` must be a base address `PageAllocate` returned, and `length` the length it was given. Succeeds when the
system accepted the release.
A `length` of zero is refused with `InvalidLength`, and a null `address` with `InvalidAddress`, rather than either
being quietly ignored: both are arithmetic errors at the caller far more often than intentions.
Every pointer into the range becomes invalid, and the address space may be handed to the next allocation at once.
Windows requires the exact base address and ignores the length entirely; the other systems accept a sub-range and
release only that, so a wrong length there silently releases the wrong amount.
doc.returns: nothing on success, or the reason the system refused the release

items.name: PageProtect
items.signature: pub func PageProtect(address: *var opaque, length: uint, protection: uint32) -> ! PageError

doc.summary: Changes what may be done with `length` bytes at `address`.
doc.markdown:
Changes what may be done with `length` bytes at `address`.
`address` must be page-aligned and `length` is rounded up to whole pages. Succeeds when the system accepted the
change.
The change takes effect at once, so a thread touching the range concurrently faults rather than finishing what it
started.
Nothing here checks that the range was ever allocated. Asking for write and execute together is refused on Apple
Silicon without an entitlement and by policy on hardened systems elsewhere, which arrives as `PermissionDenied`.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes, rounded up to whole pages

params.name: protection
params.markdown: what may be done with the pages afterwards

doc.returns: nothing on success, or the reason the system refused the change

items.name: PageAlign
items.signature: pub func PageAlign(length: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: Rounds `length` up to a whole number of `MinimumPageSize` blocks.
doc.markdown:
Rounds `length` up to a whole number of `MinimumPageSize` blocks.
It rounds to the bound rather than to the system's real page size, which is a deliberate difference from what
the name suggests and the reason `MinimumPageSize` is public. Rounding to a divisor of the real size cannot make
an allocation wrong — every call in this module hands the length to a system that rounds again, up to whatever
its pages actually are — and it keeps a file read out of an allocator's inner loop. On a machine with larger
pages the result is a length the system will round further, which costs nothing.
A caller that needs the length to be a whole number of *real* pages asks `PageSize` once, keeps the answer, and
rounds with `AlignUp` itself.
Returns the rounded length, or `length` itself when rounding would pass the end of the range — which a caller
sizing an allocation should notice, since the system will refuse such a length anyway.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: length
params.markdown: the byte count to round up

items.name: Realloc
items.signature: pub func Realloc(ptr: *opaque, size: uint) -> *var opaque

doc.summary: Resizes an allocation to `size` bytes, preserving the bytes that still fit.
doc.markdown:
Resizes an allocation to `size` bytes, preserving the bytes that still fit.
A null `ptr` behaves as `Alloc(size)`. A zero size releases a non-null allocation and returns null. On failure,
returns null and leaves the original allocation valid; on success, the original address is invalid even when the
returned address has the same numeric value.
A non-null `ptr` must be the live base address returned by `Alloc` or an earlier `Realloc`. Interior, released,
or foreign addresses are invalid. Bytes added beyond the old size are uninitialized.

params.name: ptr
params.markdown: the allocation to resize, or null to allocate

params.name: size
params.markdown: the wanted size; zero releases and returns null

doc.returns: the address of the resized allocation, or null on failure
